subsection: 3. Changes in education, health and social welfare provision

notes.h: Education: Investment in Education and the 1960s reforms
notes.b: Education was reformed from the 1960s with the aim of widening access, linked to the planned economic growth of the period.
points: Investment in Education, published in 1965, was a survey of the education system that found low participation at second level and a shortage of trained teachers.
Patrick Hillery, Minister for Education from 1959 to 1965, commissioned the survey and began the reforms that followed.
The first comprehensive school opened in 1966 at Shannon, Co. Clare; comprehensive schools took pupils of all abilities and offered a wider range of subjects.
Donogh O'Malley, Minister for Education from 1966, announced free second-level education in September 1966, with free places from 1967.
Free school transport was introduced alongside free secondary education to help rural pupils reach schools.
Equality of opportunity was the stated aim: the reforms were meant to let children from poorer families stay in education past the age of 14.

notes.h: Education: community schools, Regional Technical Colleges and third-level grants
points: Regional Technical Colleges were set up from 1970 to provide technical and vocational education outside Dublin, with the first opening in the early 1970s.
Community schools were developed from the 1970s, combining vocational and academic provision in one school and offering adult education in the community.
State grants for third-level students were extended in the 1960s and 1970s, helping students from less well-off homes to attend university or a college of technology.
A new primary curriculum was introduced in 1971, moving away from the rote learning of the earlier curriculum and placing more emphasis on children's activity and understanding.
Increased participation in second-level education meant that more young people stayed in school to take the Leaving Certificate.

notes.h: Health: the Health Act 1953 and the Voluntary Health Insurance scheme
points: The Health Act 1953 consolidated health services and set up the framework for hospital and community care.
The Voluntary Health Insurance Board (VHI) was established in 1957 to offer private health insurance to people who wanted cover for hospital treatment outside the public system.
The VHI was a voluntary scheme, so it did not cover everyone, and access depended on paying premiums.
Hospital building expanded through the 1960s, with new regional hospitals and improved facilities.
The Health Act 1970 replaced the existing structure of local health authorities with regional health boards, created in 1970 and eight in number.
The health boards were given responsibility for hospitals, community care and public health services within their areas.
The new structure aimed to make services more uniform across the country, though the quality of care still varied between regions.
Health provision was also shaped by the Mother and Child Scheme crisis of 1951, which had shown the power of the medical profession and the Catholic Church over state health policy.

notes.h: Social welfare: pensions, allowances and new benefits
points: Children's allowance was paid by the state to families with children, expanded in the 1960s and 1970s to cover more children.
Old age pensions were extended through the 1960s and 1970s, raising the level of support for elderly people with no other income.
Unemployment benefit and assistance were available to workers who lost jobs, though payments were low and eligibility was limited.
An unmarried mothers' allowance was introduced in 1973, making payments available to women who had children outside marriage (verify exact year).
The 1970s saw a rise in the number of people receiving social welfare as unemployment grew after the oil crises (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).
Local authorities built large numbers of houses in the 1960s, many of them on the edges of cities and towns.
Ballymun, north Dublin, was developed from the mid-1960s with high-rise flats that later became associated with social problems.
Suburban growth around Dublin, Cork and Limerick expanded the built-up area and changed the pattern of urban living.
Rural electrification, carried out by the Electricity Supply Board from the 1940s and largely completed by the early 1970s, brought electricity to farms and villages.
Rural water schemes were built alongside electrification to supply clean drinking water to homes that had relied on wells and streams.

notes.h: Assessment: welfare and equality of opportunity
points: Achievements: free secondary education and the expansion of comprehensive schools widened access to education, especially for students from rural and working-class families.
Limits: the VHI was a voluntary scheme and left many people without cover, and the health boards did not remove regional inequality in care.
Contemporary view: the reforms were welcomed by parents and teachers, who saw them as overdue.
Later view: historians note that the reforms widened access but did not remove class differences in attainment, and that housing schemes such as Ballymun later faced serious problems.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that access to education, health care and welfare should not depend on a person's family background, wealth or place of residence.
A second-level school that takes pupils of all abilities and offers a broad range of academic and vocational subjects.
A second-level school that combines academic, vocational and adult education in one local institution.
A third-level college set up from 1970 to provide technical and vocational education outside Dublin.
Private health cover, sold through the Voluntary Health Insurance Board from 1957, that paid for hospital treatment in return for premiums.
The policy, announced by Donogh O'Malley in 1966 and in force from 1967, of ending fees for second-level pupils.
